title: nvn: frame-step recovery gets stuck at 20/30 fps on Android when load clears
body:
## Summary

On Android (`!mtl_link_active()`), games that use host frame stepping (`FRAME_STEP`) with `fps_hold=on` (*Breath of the Wild*, *Tears of the Kingdom*, *Pokémon Legends: Z-A*, *Paper Mario: The Origami King*) can get stuck at 30 or 20 fps (`k = 2` or `k = 3`) even after GPU/CPU load drops and the scene is well within the 60 fps budget.

## Root cause

In `nxnative/dm/gfx/nvn/hle_nvn.c`, `fstep_tick` only works cleanly when a display link (`mtl_link_active()`) drives pacing waits through `pace_ns`:

1. **`pq_ns` is not subtracted when `!mtl_link_active()`:** On Android there is no display link (`pace_ns ≈ 0`); triple-buffered swapchain and async replay pacing waits accrue in `pq_ns` (`job_wait` + `mtl_present_wait`). 2. **Subtracting `pq_ns` alone would hide replay-thread saturation:** `pq_ns` also waits while `replay_main` is executing `JOB_SUBMIT` and `JOB_PRESENT`, so subtracting `pq_ns` without tracking async replay duration (`g_f

body:
# Celeste crashes on Snapdragon 680 due to ARMv8.1 LSE instructions in NVN thunks

## Environment
- **nx2android version:** v0.4.0
- **Device:** OPPO A78 4G
- **SoC:** Qualcomm Snapdragon 680
- **GPU:** Adreno 610
- **Architecture:** ARM64 (`arm64-v8a`)
- **Android version:** Android 15
- **Game:** Celeste (`org.nx2a.celeste`)

## Problem

Celeste repeatedly crashed shortly after launch on the Snapdragon 680.

The original native crash logs showed:

```text
Fatal signal 4 (SIGILL)
code 1 (ILL_ILLOPC)
```

The reported program counter was:

```text
libdmhost.so + 0x192dd0
```

Original library Build ID:

```text
1df6226ed984d2e0
```

## Investigation

With assistance from ChatGPT, I investigated the native crash and inspected the ARM64 instructions in `libdmhost.so`.

We identified multiple ARMv8.1-A LSE atomic instructions, particularly:

```asm
stadd x17, [x16]
```

These were present in the generated NVN thunk assembly:

```text
nxnative/dm/gfx/nvn/nvn_thunks.S
```

The generator responsible for this file was:

```text
nxnative/dm/gfx/tools/gen_protos.py
```

Its comments explicitly state that the generated thunks use ARMv8.1 LSE instructions.

The Snapdragon 680's reported CPU f
resolution:
Thanks for the precise report and the tested workaround. This is fixed by 7cd66c36 (fix(nvn): count NVN calls without LSE atomics), in the next release: the generated NVN thunks and the DM_NVN_PROF timing entry now use an ARMv8.0 ldxr/stxr loop instead of stadd. The only LSE instructions left in libdmhost.so are the compiler's outline-atomic helpers, which check for LSE at run time. We could not test it on an ARMv8.0 device ourselves; please build the host from main (or wait for the next release) and reopen this issue if Celeste still crashes on the Snapdragon 680.

```
Device: Retroid Pocket 6 (Android handheld, built-in gamepad), docked 1920x1080
Tool: nx2android, current main, ported on Windows
Game: FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE `[number]F12000`, update v65536 (1.0.1)

The game boots and plays, but the in-game **System Menu** (opened with **+**) ignores every face button. The D-pad moves the selection, but **A, B, X, Y, L, R, ZL, ZR, +, −, L3 and R3 do nothing**, so the menu can be neither confirmed (A) nor closed (B) and the game cannot be resumed. ```
```

```
Tried the resolution angle: it is not the cause.

- Handheld mode (`docked=0`, `DM_OPMODE=0`): the game switches to its 1280x720 profile and now polls `GetNpadState(Handheld, id 0x20)` instead of `GetNpadState(FullKey, id 0)`. D-pad still moves the cursor, A/B still do nothing in the System Menu. So it is not the npad id/style either.
- 480p: `DM_RENDER_SCALE=0.6667` is a no-op for this game (it only feeds the rewriter's render-scale stubs, which exist for TotK/BotW, not FF Resonance); the target stays 1280x720.

title: Pokemon Z-A and Scarlet: trees, rocks, street furniture and building façades missing on Vulkan: indirect draws get `c0[0x644]` (base instance) = 0. One-line fix in dmsh_xlate
body:
**Setup:** nx2android v0.3.0, Poco F6 (Adreno), Mesa Turnip 27 R2 via `--vulkan-driver`, 30 fps. Tested on Pokémon Legends: Z-A 2.0.2 (0100F43008C44000) and Pokémon Scarlet 4.0.0 (0100A3D008C5C000).

**Symptom:**
- Z-A: trees, street furniture and two opposite façades of a building near Lumiose station were not rendered (the roof was), identical from both sides. No crash, 28–32 fps.
- Scarlet: the same class of bug. Rocks and walls were invisible (the player collided with them) and trees were missing in some places.

GLSLC-compiled vertex shaders compute the absolute instance index as `(gl_InstanceIndex − gl_BaseInstance) + c0[0x644]`. GPU-culled draws (a compute pass fills the indirect records with each object's instance index in `baseInstance`, as Z-A does) therefore all read instance 0. This is the same gap as seedds/nxnative#563 (iOS/Metal, fixed in commit 8fa9b2d1 in `dmsh_build.py`).

title: porter: a merged NSP (base game and update in one file) ports as the base game; the update inside is dropped without a warning
body:
Follow-up from #156, as suggested there.

### What happens
NSP merge tools write a game's base, its update and sometimes its DLC into one file (`Game [B+U262144].nsp`, or "(1G+1U)" merges). Such a file holds one content set per title: a CNMT and a ticket for the base (`…000`), another for the update (`…800`), and so on.

`scan_nsps` gives each file a single title. Since #156, `title_of` collects every ticket in the file and returns the smallest, so a merged file is read as the base game. The update inside it is never extracted, and nothing in the log says so.

### Seen with
- **Pokémon Legends: Arceus**, base and update v262144 in one 6.55 GB NSP. `porter inspect` said `packs v0 (versions in the folder: v0) … not a version the profile was brought up on (v262144): it is packed from a derived profile`. That was on main before #156, where the file's first ticket happened to be the base game's. By the code, #156 reads it the same way.
- Before #156, `title_of` took the first ticket, so depending on file order such a file could also fail with `no base game NSP found` (per the review on #156).

### Workaround
Split the file along its CNMTs into a base NSP and an update NSP, a plain PFS0
resolution: This is fixed by 03d1fb49 (feat(porter): merged dumps (base game, update and DLC in one file) port as their version (#452)), in the next release. Please update and reopen this issue if it still happens.
```

title: Discussion: shared Android game library and on-device game preparation
body:
Hi! Building on #18, what do you think about a single Android app with a game library and on-device game preparation?

The idea would be:

- One shared compatibility layer, with versioned per-game profiles and build-specific patches kept separately.
- Import the player's own XCI/NSP and keys on the phone, then prepare and store each game in app-specific storage.
- Keep saves per game, with export/import; normal app updates retain data.
- Preserve the existing desktop porting workflow as an option.

Shared fixes would stay in the core when they implement general Switch or Vulkan behavior. Game- or build-specific choices would live in profiles; a profile update that changes code rewriting or shaders could require reprocessing the affected files.

title: Metroid Dread: dynamic lighting is missing in darker rooms - light sources do not light the scene, Samus renders black (vs Switch 2 comparison)
body:
Metroid Dread on Android loses all diffuse/ambient lighting in darker rooms: only emissive sources and direct highlights survive, everything else crushes to near-black. Samus herself renders as a black silhouette. It is clearly visible in-game (light sources do not light the room, cutscene bosses are unreadable) and reproducible on two devices here.

## Comparison against real hardware (same scene, same room)

The room with the two E.M.M.I. and the glowing pillar, same file (missiles 17/17, energy 99, same minimap position):

Android port (vivo iPA2691, `screencap` = raw framebuffer, not the panel):

![android](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SherryChaos/gh-issue-attachments/master/metroid-dread-android-vivo.png)

Switch 2 (same spot):

![ns2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SherryChaos/gh-issue-attachments/master/metroid-dread-switch2.png)

On the Switch 2 shot Samus and the room's mid-tones are clearly visible; on the Android framebuffer the same Samus position is a black shape and the walls/floor around the light sources are crushed.

Luminance of the two frames (game area only):

| | mean | median | p95 | pixels > 64 | pixels > 128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Android port
resolution:
Thanks for the detailed report and the Switch 2 comparison: the luminance table pointed straight at a missing light term.

**Cause.** It was not shadows or the swapchain. Dread's material shaders write the image-based ambient light into the light buffer during the G-buffer pass, and the deferred lights add on top of it. The ambient comes from the room's light cube maps (128x128 and 64x64 BC6H, plus a 256x256 BC1). The game fills their memory *before* it creates their memory pool (a `CPU_NO_ACCESS` pool), and the textures have no packaged layout. NVN takes those bytes as the pool's content, but the Vulkan host created the images empty at first use. Dumped on the device, every face of both cube maps was 0, so the ambient term was 0 everywhere: only emissive surfaces and direct light survived

title: Octopath Traveler fails
body:
**Title:** Android: Octopath Traveler (010057D[number]) blocked — legacy UE4.18 pak shaders require Mac host boot/decode (`DM_OODLE_SERVE`)

**Body:**

### Summary
Using the Android port of `nx2android` on *Octopath Traveler* stops during build with a clear limitation: the game requires booting in the Mac host to decode legacy Unreal pak shaders, and the Android port cannot run that step yet.

### Environment
- Tool: `nx2android` Android port
- Game: OCTOPATH TRAVELER
- Title ID: `010057D[number]`
- Update: `010057D[number]` v327680
- App version detected: `1.0.5` (`org.nx2a.t010057d[number]`)

### Steps to reproduce
1. Run `nx2android` on Android with the base NSP + update NSP above.
2. Allow it to generate the survey and provisional game profile.
3. Proceed to the build/extraction stage.

### Actual result
Build stops with:

```text
OCTOPATH TRAVELER needs a step that boots the game in the Mac host
(2 legacy Unreal pak(s) (version 4, UE 4.18: DRAGON QUEST XI S):
the shaders are inline in the cooked packages, compressed in the pak;
the shader split decodes them with the game's own decoder in the Mac host
(dm/host/hle_oodle.c DM_OODLE_SERVE)), which the Android port cannot run yet
resolution:
Ported and running on Android now: #76.

**Cause.** The survey took OCTOPATH TRAVELER's legacy Unreal paks for DRAGON QUEST XI S's LZ5 ones, which need the game's own decoder in the Mac host. Its blocks are plain zlib (`Kingship-Switch.pak`, 103,018 files). The porter now decodes them itself, so the shader split runs on Windows / Linux too: 5,434 shaders, all translated.

**What else it needed:**
- **Rewriter:** a jump table with a 64-bit bounds check (`main+0x1676f58`).
- **NVN:**
  - the sparse tile layout queries;
  - a virtual pool per streamed texture, read through its page table on Android, where `vm_remap` cannot alias memory;
```

body:
## Summary

`porter`'s `version_code()` is `nsp.vnum(ver) + 1` (`porter/pipeline.py`). Rebuilding the **same** game version (e.g. after a host/shader fix, or a re-extract with the newer toolchain) produces an APK with the **same versionCode**. Android then treats it as an identical package: `adb install -r` fails with `INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE` only if the signer changed, but with the same signer a plain `adb install -r` **replaces** the app — yet if the user wants to keep the old install as a fallback, or the rebuild must install over an older *different* build, the same versionCode blocks `adb install -r` (it downgrades/conflicts) unless the app is uninstalled first (which **wipes the save data**).

title: android: a save export / import in the pause menu, so a port keeps the progress of the real console
body:
# android: a save export / import in the pause menu, so a port keeps the progress of the real console

The Android port has no way to move a save in or out of the app. A player who
already has progress on a real Switch cannot continue it on the phone, and a
player who has progress on the phone loses it with one uninstall or one
`--replace-signer`. Both directions matter, and both are ordinary things a
player expects of a port. This asks for them as a feature, and records what
was measured while doing the two transfers by hand, because the numbers decide
how the feature should be built.

Related: #3 asks the same question in one line, from the emulator side. This
issue is the same request with the measurements.

## Why it is needed

1. **Progress does not move between the console and the phone.** The ports run
   the game's own code, so the save a port writes is the console's save, byte
   for byte. Nothing in the format stops it from being copied out and back.
   Only the plumbing is missing.
2. **Saves are in a place no player can reach.** `front_android.c:725` puts
   `DM_SAVE` at `act->internalDataPath` + `/save`, that is
   `/data/user/0/<package>/files/sav
resolution:
We already built a small version of this, before opening the issue. It is not
in upstream and it is not a pull request: it lives on a branch of our fork and
was checked on the device. This comment is to describe what it does and to ask
whether the direction is one you would take, so that a proper version can
follow the shape you want rather than ours.

## What it does

Two rows in the existing pause menu, next to the settings that are already
there: **Export save** and **Import save**. Both are front-end only
(`dm/android/front_android.c`); nothing reaches the game, and there is no
profile key.

**Export** copies the committed save tree (`DM_SAVE`, and `<DM_SAVE>_device`
when a game mounts both, `hle_fs.c` line 495) to
`Download/nx2android/<package>/<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>/`, one folder per expo

body:
**Device:** Red Magic Astra (NP05J), Snapdragon 8 Elite / Adreno 830, Android 16
**Game:** Castlevania: Belmont's Curse (0100BA4026E94000), built on Windows with `porter port --experimental` (provisional profile)
**Base:** 421fe06

On 421fe06 the game settles at 30 fps. Its own load is small: on the cpu0–5 cluster it needs only 1.0–1.8 GHz to hold 60. Two host bugs held it down, and both should affect every game. With the two fixes below it runs at a steady 60 fps on the tablet, with the on-screen gamepad shown or hidden.

### 1. The adaptive frame rate counted the present wait as frame work
The adaptive rate picks 60 / 40 / 30 from the frame work. That work included the time the present thread spends waiting for its slot (the acquire wait in `hle_nvn.c`), which is display pacing, not load. Once the rate dropped to 40 or 30 (a loading screen is enough), every frame included the longer wait. Work then looked like 25–33 ms, and the rate could never step back up.

On Super Mario Odyssey's menu it stayed at 30 with about 1 ms of GPU work per frame. `DM_FPS_PIN=60` gave 60 at once.

**Fix:** pass the present wait separately (`pq_ns`). `perf_android.c` judges late or not-late on the work

title: Vulkan present darkens games whose window texture is sRGB (blit from SRGB image into UNORM swapchain)
body:
## Summary Games that present an sRGB window texture show a dark, low-contrast picture on Android. The present path copies the window texture into the swapchain with `vkCmdBlitImage`. The swapchain is always created as `VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM`, so a blit from an `R8G8B8A8_SRGB` image decodes the texels to linear and stores them unencoded. This removes the sRGB transfer curve, so mid-tones and shadows come out too dark. On the Switch, the window texture's bytes are scanned out unchanged. Games whose window texture is UNORM are not affected, which is likely why the current Android profiles look correct. ## Observed in Donkey Kong Country Returns HD The game boots and plays at full speed (60 fps), with no errors in the log, but the whole picture looks too dark and flat. Lit areas lose their brightness, shadows and mid-tones sink, and the scenes lack the contrast and depth they have on the Switch, so the lighting looks wrong even though every lighting pass renders. With the fix below, the picture matches the Switch.
Screenshots: before and after the fix | Before (UNORM swapchain) | After (sRGB swapchain) | |---|---| |
